                    ### Question
                    A 56-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of pain and swelling in his left leg. He has a history of pancreatic cancer and is currently receiving chemotherapy. Three weeks ago, he had a similar episode in his right arm that resolved without treatment. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Palpation of the left leg shows a tender, cord-shaped structure medial to the medial condyle of the femur. The overlying skin is erythematous. Which of the following vessels is most likely affected?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Anterior tibial artery
opb. Superficial femoral artery
opc. Great saphenous vein
opd. External iliac vein
ope. Deep femoral vein

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with pain, swelling, and erythema in the left leg, alongside a history of pancreatic cancer and chemotherapy, which significantly increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). The tender, cord-like structure palpated in the leg suggests thrombosis, likely deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Given the location and symptoms, the deep femoral vein is a common site for DVT, especially in cancer patients. While the great saphenous vein is also a potential site for thrombosis, the deep femoral vein is more commonly affected in this context. The presence of fever further supports the possibility of an inflammatory process associated with thrombosis. Therefore, the most likely affected vessel is the deep femoral vein.
